sanskrit: अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम ।
नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते ॥
translit: asmākaṁ tu viśhiṣhṭā ye tānnibodha dwijottama
nāyakā mama sainyasya sanjñārthaṁ tānbravīmi te
theme: Now Look at Our Own Team
hindi: हे द्विजश्रेष्ठ (द्रोणाचार्य)! अब हमारी ओर जो विशेष योद्धा हैं, उन्हें भी जान लीजिए। आपकी जानकारी के लिए मैं अपनी सेना के उन नायकों के नाम बताता हूँ।
english: Duryodhana says: “O best of the twice-born, now also know the chief warriors on our side, the leaders of my army. I will name them for your information.”
deeper: After describing the Pandava heroes in verses 1.4 to 1.6, Duryodhana now turns to his own side. The little word tu (“but” or “and now”) marks this turn. He has looked at the other army; now he looks at his own. Preparing for a big task means knowing both: what stands in front of you and what you have with you.

He calls Drona dvijottama, “best of the twice-born”, a respectful title. He says he is naming his leaders sanjñārtham, “for your information”. Yet Drona already knows these warriors well. Many readers see a king who is a little anxious and keeps talking, hoping his teacher will feel reassured. Words spoken from worry sound different from words spoken from calm confidence.

For us, the verse is a gentle lesson. It is good to know your team, to value each person’s strength, and to be clear about who is helping you. But a list of names cannot give peace of mind. Real strength comes from a clear heart and doing the right thing, and the Gita will teach us more about that as it goes on.
background: The great war of Kurukshetra is about to begin. Duryodhana, the Kaurava prince, has looked at the Pandava army standing in battle formation and has gone to his teacher Drona. He points out the mighty Pandava warriors one by one: Bhima, Arjuna, Yuyudhana, Virata, Drupada, and others (1.4–1.6), including Abhimanyu and the sons of Draupadi.

Having named the strong warriors on the other side, Duryodhana now changes direction. In this verse he begins to speak about the leaders of his own army. The names themselves follow in the next verses (1.8 onwards).
lessons: Before a big task, it helps to know who is with you and what each person can do.
Seeing the challenge is only half the work; seeing your own strengths and gaps is the other half.
Duryodhana addresses Drona politely, and speaking respectfully to elders is always a good habit.
When we talk too much to win approval, it may be because we feel unsure inside.
Strength is more than a list
Names and numbers help, but a calm mind and a right purpose matter even more.
examples: Before the school match, Kabir’s captain reads out each player’s strength: Imran bowls fast and Neha fields well. Knowing his team makes him feel ready.
Ananya’s group has a science project. She asks who draws well, who writes neatly and who speaks clearly. Everyone gets a job that suits them.
Rohan keeps telling his coach about his team’s good players before a race. Then he notices he is nervous. He takes three slow breaths and feels steadier.
Meera asks her teacher, “Ma’am, may I explain our plan to you?” Her respectful tone makes the teacher happy to listen.
Before the school play, Arjun checks not only the other class’s costumes but also his own class’s dialogues. Then he rehearses his lines once more.
After the hockey match, Simran names every teammate and says what each one did well. The whole team smiles.
Dev keeps looking at how fast his cousin solves puzzles. His mother says, “Look at what you can do well too.” Dev then tries his own way and enjoys it.
Before a school trip, Tara checks the list: water bottle, cap, notebook. She does not only worry about the weather; she makes sure her own bag is ready.

story.title: Meera and the Kabaddi Captain’s Speech
paras: In a small town near Pune, Meera was made captain of her school kabaddi team. The next day they would play against the strongest team in the district. That evening Meera went to her coach, Sir, and began talking very fast.

“Sir, their raider Kavya is very quick, and their defenders are tall,” she said. Then she added, “But now look at our team! Pooja is the best at tackles, Ishita is fast, and Sneha never gives up. Sir, let me tell you everyone’s strengths!” Coach listened kindly, though he already knew his players well.

When she finished, he smiled and said, “Meera, I know your team. But I think you are saying all this to calm your own heart.” Meera blushed, then laughed. “Yes, Sir. I am a little afraid.” Coach said, “It is good to know your team. Now also trust them, and play honestly.”

The next day Meera did not rattle off lists. She took a deep breath, looked at her friends, and said, “Let us play our best and play fair.” They played well. They did not win every raid, but they played together and went home proud.
story.moral: Lesson: Knowing your team’s strengths is wise, but a calm heart and trust in each other matter even more than a long list of names.

quiz.q: Whom is Duryodhana speaking to in this verse?
quiz.x: Duryodhana addresses his teacher Drona as “dvijottama”.

quiz.q: What does Duryodhana say he will do now?
o: Name the leaders of his own army
quiz.x: He says he will name the chief leaders of his own army “for your information”.

quiz.q: What does the little word “tu” (“but, and now”) show in this verse?
o: He turns from the other side to his own side
quiz.x: After describing the Pandava warriors, he now shifts attention to his own warriors.

quiz.q: Which everyday lesson fits this verse best?
o: Only count the other team’s strengths
Know your own team and stay calm
quiz.x: The verse reminds us to know our own side, while a calm mind gives the deeper strength.

reel.hook: Why does a prince list his own warriors right after counting enemies?
reel.lesson: Know your own team’s strengths too, not just how strong the others look.
reel.caption:
Duryodhana turns from the other army to his own in Gita 1.7. 🛡️
Know your team, trust your team, and stay calm inside.
Who is on YOUR team today? 💛
